clue.text: Tries to enter bona fide practice

indicators.note: one piece is said to go into the other, so the trial-hearing word sits inside the genuine word

parts.note: bona fide means real, genuine
a court tries a case, that is, hears it

explanation.surface: Someone attempts to get into genuine practice of a profession.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tries' is not attempts but the courtroom sense: a judge hears a case.
explanation.definitionFit: A rehearsal is a practice run before a performance.

clue.text: Memorial of old priest outwardly Roman Catholic

indicators.note: the Catholic abbreviation stands on the outside, around the priest

parts.note: Eli is the Old Testament priest who raised Samuel

explanation.surface: A memorial to an ancient priest who was outwardly a Catholic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outwardly' looks like a comment on the priest's faith, but it tells you the Catholic abbreviation wraps around him. Eli is the Old Testament priest who raised Samuel.
explanation.definitionFit: A relic is an object kept in memory of a saint or the past, a memorial.

clue.text: The arms go round one's pet

indicators.note: the letters circulate and come back in a new order

explanation.surface: Someone's arms encircle their pet in a hug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'go round' sounds like a hug; it reshuffles THE ARMS.
explanation.definitionFit: A hamster is a small rodent commonly kept as a pet.

clue.text: In any case, a refusal will not please

indicators.note: a case holds something, so the word any encloses the refusal

parts.note: taken as written
no is a refusal

explanation.surface: A refusal will displease, whatever the circumstances.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In any case' reads as 'anyway'; 'case' is the container around NO.
explanation.definitionFit: To annoy someone is to displease or irritate them.

clue.text: Showed no respect and ate greedily

definitions.meaning: to scoff at is to mock or treat with contempt
to scoff food is British slang for wolfing it down

explanation.surface: Someone was rude and gobbled their food.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb has two senses: mocked with derision, and devoured greedily in British slang.

clue.text: After something to drink, had a meal to finish off

indicators.note: the meal word comes after the drink word in the answer

parts.note: a liquid is something one drinks
ate means had a meal

explanation.surface: After a drink, someone eats a meal to round things off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finish off' sounds like completing dinner but means kill.
explanation.definitionFit: To liquidate is to wipe out or kill, to finish off.

clue.text: They were widely worn in Oxford in the '20s

definitions.text: They were widely worn in Oxford in the '20s

parts.words: They were widely worn in Oxford in the '20s
parts.note: reads as university fashion history; refers to the very wide-legged trousers fashionable with Oxford undergraduates in the 1920s

explanation.surface: A piece of fashion history about what students wore at Oxford a century ago.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Widely' is the joke: the trousers were famously wide in the leg, not merely popular.
explanation.definitionFit: Oxford bags were baggy trousers, and bags is a British word for loose trousers.

clue.text: Stop for Jack to revive

definitions.meaning: Jack is a sailor; in nautical terms a vessel is brought to a halt

explanation.surface: A halt is called so that Jack can be revived.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack, like tar, is a crossword sailor: bringing a ship to is stopping it at sea.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both stopping a ship and making someone conscious again.

clue.text: Fashion model glad to win first prize

indicators.note: to fashion is to shape, so these letters are reshaped into a new order

explanation.surface: A fashion model is delighted to come first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fashion' reads as the industry; it is a verb rearranging MODEL GLAD.
explanation.definitionFit: A gold medal is awarded for first place in a competition.

clue.text: Wading bird? It's a ruddy duck!

parts.note: ruddy is a mild British expletive, like flaming or bloody
a duck is a zero score in cricket, hence the letter O

explanation.surface: A birdwatcher's confusion: is that wader actually a ruddy duck, a real species?
explanation.walkthrough: The ruddy duck is a genuine bird, which makes the surface plausible; here 'ruddy' is the swear word and 'duck' the nought.
explanation.definitionFit: The flamingo is a long-legged pink bird that wades in shallow lakes.

clue.text: Top flight writers long out of fashion?

definitions.text: Top flight writers long out of fashion?

parts.words: Top flight writers long out of fashion?
parts.note: reads as authors whose best days are past; really the big flight feathers of a bird, once cut into pens for writing

explanation.surface: Wondering whether first-rate authors have long since gone out of style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top flight' seems to mean excellent but literally names the main feathers used in flying, which were the old writing pens.
explanation.definitionFit: Large wing feathers were sharpened into pens, the writing tools of earlier centuries.

clue.text: Volatile feline put in an enclosure

indicators.note: the feline is placed inside the enclosure, one piece going into another

parts.note: a sty is an enclosure for pigs
a cat is a feline

explanation.surface: An excitable cat has been shut in a pen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Volatile' reads as describing the cat but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Scatty is British informal for scatterbrained and flighty, unpredictable in mood.

clue.text: Aunt Sally, for example, may be legitimate prey

definitions.meaning: Aunt Sally is a traditional British pub and fairground game of throwing sticks at a dummy's head
something or someone that may properly be hunted or attacked

explanation.surface: A relative called Sally might be a fair target for attack.
explanation.walkthrough: Aunt Sally is a fairground game, and by extension a figure set up to be criticised, which links both senses.
explanation.definitionFit: Fair game is an idiom for a person or thing open to attack or ridicule, and a fairground game literally.

clue.text: Search the bed again for source of provocation

parts.note: re- is the prefix meaning again
to drag a river or lake is to search its bed with hooks or a net

explanation.surface: Searching under the mattress again might provoke someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The bed' looks like furniture, but the bed is that of a river or lake, searched by dragging.
explanation.definitionFit: A red rag, as waved at a bull, is an idiom for anything sure to provoke anger.

clue.text: One thus may show soppy demeanour

definitions.text: One thus may show soppy demeanour

indicators.note: soppy means sloppily soft, so the letters are made mushy and rearranged

explanation.surface: A person in this state may behave in a soppy way.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines: someone smitten shows soppy behaviour.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone in love tends to act sentimentally, showing a soppy manner.

clue.text: Such a monster caused the death of Desdemona

definitions.text: Such a monster caused the death of Desdemona

parts.words: Such a monster caused the death of Desdemona
parts.note: in Othello Iago warns of jealousy as a monster with a colour for its eyes; jealousy drives Othello to kill Desdemona

explanation.surface: A remark about the tragedy of Shakespeare's Othello.
explanation.walkthrough: Iago calls jealousy 'the green-eyed monster', and Othello's jealousy leads him to kill his wife Desdemona.
explanation.definitionFit: The hyphenated adjective means jealous, from Shakespeare's image of jealousy as a monster.

clue.text: Suit worn by the wealthy

definitions.meaning: one of the four suits in a pack of playing cards
precious gems that rich people wear as jewellery

explanation.surface: An outfit favoured by rich people.
explanation.definitionFit: One card suit has the red lozenge symbol, and the costly gemstones are worn as jewellery by the rich.

clue.text: Dude pals prepare to ride on the ranch

definitions.text: Dude pals prepare to ride on the ranch

indicators.note: to prepare is to put things in order, so these letters are reorganised

explanation.surface: Cowboy friends get ready for a ride on the ranch.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: on a dude ranch, the pals preparing to ride do just this.
explanation.definitionFit: To saddle up is to put a saddle on a horse before riding, typical cowboy talk.

clue.text: I'm cold — I move home

indicators.note: the letters are moved around into a new order

explanation.surface: Feeling chilly, someone decides to move house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'move' reshuffles IMCOLD plus I.
explanation.definitionFit: A domicil, usually domicile, is a legal term for one's permanent home.

clue.text: One is prone to use arms in this exercise

definitions.text: One is prone to use arms in this exercise

parts.words: One is prone to use arms in this exercise
parts.note: reads like a soldier inclined to weapons drill; really lying face down pushing up with the arms

explanation.surface: Sounds like a soldier keen to handle weapons on drill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'prone' means lying face down, not inclined; 'arms' are limbs, not weapons.
explanation.definitionFit: The exercise means lying face down and pushing the body up with the arms.

clue.text: Get out of breath, being no longer fit

parts.note: ex- means former, no longer
hale means healthy, fit

explanation.surface: Someone panting because they are not as fit as they used to be.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get out of breath' sounds like panting but literally means send breath out.
explanation.definitionFit: To exhale is to breathe out, expelling breath from the lungs.

clue.text: Beats a side from London

definitions.meaning: the nickname of West Ham United, a London football club

explanation.surface: A London team defeats its opponents.
explanation.walkthrough: West Ham United are a London football team known as the Hammers.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means pounds or strikes, and is the nickname of West Ham United football club.

clue.text: Hundred men come prepared to start

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred

indicators.note: prepared as in made up or worked into shape, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A hundred men arrive ready to begin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'prepared' makes OMMENCE from MEN COME, placed after C.
explanation.definitionFit: Commence is a formal synonym for begin.

clue.text: Scholar meets master primarily to express disapproval of cane

parts.note: a BA is a Bachelor of Arts, a scholar

indicators.note: primarily signals taking just the first letter of master

parts.note: to boo is to jeer in disapproval

explanation.surface: A student and a schoolmaster object to the use of the cane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cane' suggests school punishment, fitting the scholar and master, but is the plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Bamboo is a tall grass with woody hollow stems, commonly called cane.

clue.text: Two support the church

parts.note: a bra is a supporting undergarment
CE stands for the Church of England

explanation.surface: Two people prop up the church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'support' is the undergarment, not a backer.
explanation.definitionFit: A brace is a pair, as in a brace of pheasants.

clue.text: Working to finish without pause or interruption

parts.note: on means working, operating
end means finish

explanation.surface: Working until the job is finished, without a break.
explanation.definitionFit: On end is an idiom meaning continuously, as in hours on end.

clue.text: Put in charge in quarry that's steep

indicators.note: the second in says where the charge abbreviation goes: inside the hunted animal word

parts.note: quarry is the hunted animal, prey
IC is the standard abbreviation for in charge; someone put in charge is IC

explanation.surface: Someone placed in charge of a quarry finds the job tough.
explanation.walkthrough: 'quarry' suggests a stone pit; here it is the hunted animal. 'steep' means expensive.
explanation.definitionFit: Steep is informal for overpriced, which is what pricey means.

clue.text: Masefield's mal-de-mer?

parts.note: reads as the poet suffering seasickness; really his famous poem of longing for the ocean, read as an illness of the waves

explanation.surface: Wondering whether the poet John Masefield got seasick.
explanation.walkthrough: John Masefield's best-known poem begins 'I must go down to the seas again'; its title, taken literally, sounds like a maritime ailment.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of the Masefield poem names a passion for the ocean, playfully read as nausea on the waves.

clue.text: An image I'd behold in retrospect

parts.note: taken as written, the apostrophe dropped

indicators.note: looking back, so the word for behold is read backwards

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning look, behold

explanation.surface: An image that I'd look back upon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'behold' seems a mere verb of looking, but its archaic one-word equivalent supplies letters; 'in retrospect' signals looking backwards, so that little word is turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: An idol is an image of a god used as an object of worship.

clue.text: Urge to go into action when disheartened

indicators.note: one piece goes into the other, the urging word inside the action word

parts.note: a deed is an action
to press is to urge

explanation.surface: A call to get moving at a moment of low spirits.
explanation.definitionFit: Depressed and disheartened both mean low in spirit.
